The figure shows five boxes and the three flip cards show three things, so the count of six (two tools counted separately) is hard to check.
The three zoom levels are a clear idea once read, but they come as three long paragraphs with quotes and attributions, which is a heavy first read.
“Agentic system” and “agent” differ by one word, and the difference only becomes clear in the next sentence.
The Learn text calls the client “your connection to the model”. The key is never passed in, and the fact that OpenAI() reads OPENAI_API_KEY by itself is explained only in the quiz feedback, after the

The stray spaces between AI and 智能体 make the line read like a word-for-word translation.
The doubled braces look like a typo. They are f-string escapes, and the lesson never says so, so a newcomer may think the code is broken.
The code never links the answers list to the competitors list. That link (number N is list item N minus 1) is explained only in the Step 4 walk-through and the quiz feedback, not in the code.
The reply is never stored or printed, so the reader cannot see that the local model worked.
The ** unpacking is first used here, but the lesson only explains it in Lesson 6.
A blank sits in the code, and the instruction to fill it appears only in the quiz after the code.
The wrapper with type and function appears with no word on why the model needs it.
app.py, the chat page that calls the model, is never shown, so a newcomer cannot rebuild the final app from the lesson.
The code's message is “Someone wants to get in touch”, not this text, and the card's note says the push is printed without the keys, which the code never does.
The function calls push(), but no line imports it, and the default values are not explained.
The trap is named, but 'accuracy' and why the last 10 percent is costly are never explained before this list.
'Pilot' and 'vendor' are used in the trap list without a definition, so a newcomer has to guess what they mean.
The lesson says to judge by one number but never shows what such a number looks like.
The lesson just before this one is the budget lesson, not the map. The thread skips it, and 'you' here differs from the names used elsewhere.
The three-to-five link is never shown, so a newcomer cannot see where 'budget' or 'data' come from.
Earlier lessons call her Rohani 女士. A Chinese reader may think this is a different person.
The lesson opens on terms it never explains (large language model, retrieval, latency). Ironically, that is the exact problem the lesson is about.
AI agent appears for the first time here, with no explanation. Failure modes is also new.
The table is English only, so a 中文 reader gets the rows with no explanation. The phrase data leaves us is also unclear.

confusing.where: Step 2, intro line above the sorting game
confusing.why: The sorting game shows four tasks, so a careful reader stops to ask where the fifth one went.
The title says AI and agents, but the lesson never says what an agent is, so the link between the helper and the word agent is missing.
A limit is stated with no name and no reason. A newcomer cannot look it up or know when it applies.
The quote is also the model's output, so it can be invented too. A newcomer would trust the quote without checking it.
The $2,400 appears from nowhere. I cannot see how it was counted, and the $3,000 overtime figure needs the $30 an hour from the game in Step 2.
The sort game uses the words hard saving and soft benefit, but the Learn text never names the two groups as a pair, so soft is only implied.
ROI is in the title but never spelled out in English. The 中文 says 投资回报率, so the English reader is left guessing.
'Train' is used before it is explained. A newcomer does not know what training a model means.
This step has six definitions and no Test box, so the reader is never asked to check they understood. Every other step has one.

Jason is not introduced anywhere in this lesson or in its story, so the analogy names a stranger.
The shelf-label project is never named. The reader cannot tell what it is or whether it is the Step 1 price-label pilot.
Model size and cost are used as if they were the same idea, but the lesson never said what makes a model big or why it costs more per call.
A specific '10 times' reads like a law of nature, but the lesson gives no source for it.
'Price per unit of ability' is vague and 'frontier models' is never explained.
Here 'agent' means a human support worker. Lesson 1 taught 'agent' as an AI, so the word clashes.
Plumbing means pipes. Fridges are equipment, so the analogy does not show what 'plumbing' means for AI tools.
The word 'prompt' is used as if I already know it. The sorting game then uses 'Better prompt' as one of its three answers, so I could not sort anything without knowing what it means.

confusing.where: Step 4 · Combine them, and ask for proof
confusing.why: Mr Tan appears here for the first time, with no role. I only learn later, in the warning box, that he made a mistake in his first week.
The hero says 'Devi's team', but the story never says who Devi is. I do not know if Devi is a builder, a boss, or someone else.
A newcomer does not yet know what the model is or what a paid call to it means, so the cost list starts with a word they cannot place.
Read literally it sounds like a table row, and the 中文 reads like a word-for-word translation of that phrase.
Step 2 said S$0.30 is the whole task cost, and checking time was never priced. The quiz then counts checking inside the same S$0.30, so the numbers do not match.
A newcomer who does not know kopi o or kaya toast loses the scene. The 中文 renders kopi o as 咖啡乌, which a reader will not recognise as coffee.

confusing.where: Story and Back at the mart
confusing.why: The company is never named until the last callout, and Devi first appears as the person who can say stop in Step 4 with no introduction. I did not know who she was.
A new shop name appears out of nowhere. The story calls it 'the mart' run by Mdm Rohani, so a newcomer wonders if this is a different company.
Five roles are listed, but the product owner is never named. The reader has to guess that Auntie Lim is the product owner.
